study.title: Psalms 86 - Prayer of confidence amid distress
study.overview: Psalm 86 gathers supplication, confession of faith and praise in a prayer attributed to David. The psalmist presents himself as a poor, afflicted and dependent servant, asking God to hear him, preserve him and save him. At the same time, he bases his hope on the character of God: good, forgiving, merciful, late to anger and abundant in goodness and truth. The psalm also looks beyond the personal crisis and states that the nations will recognize the greatness of the Lord. The prayer ends by asking for a visible sign of divine favor, so that enemies may see and be ashamed.

outline.title: supplication of an afflicted servant
outline.explanation: In the first verses, David asks God to incline his ear, preserve his soul, and have mercy on him. The insistence on praying every day shows urgency and perseverance, while the self-image of a dedicated servant reveals dependence and covenant with God.

outline.title: The foundation of the request: who God is
outline.explanation: Prayer rests on the character of the Lord, described as good, forgiving and unique in power. The psalmist asks instruction to walk in the truth, promises to praise God with all their hearts and anticipates that all nations will worship him. The memory of the deliverance of death strengthens confidence in divine mercy.

outline.title: Conflict with the arrogant and request of a sign
outline.explanation: The latter part contrasts violent and arrogant enemies with the compassionate and faithful God. David asks for strength, salvation, and a sign of kindness that humbles the adversaries. The outcome unites suffering, consolation and public witness of God's help.

study.context: The notes indicate that this is the only psalm attached to David in the third book of Psalms. They also present it as a proper prayer for times of distress, especially under persecution or slander. The psalm does not depend on a specific historical scenario explained in the text; its form allows repeated use in the devotional life of God's people.
study.theology: The Psalm teaches that biblical prayer is not only a request, but also worship and trust in the character of God. The basis of the psalmist's hope is not his own strength, but rather the goodness, forgiveness, faithfulness and mercy of the Lord. He asks for moral instruction and inner unity: an undivided heart in reverent fear. The claim that the nations will prostrate before God broadens the vision of salvation beyond Israel and announces the universality of the divine lordship. The opposition between the violent and the compassionate God shows that judgment and consolation belong to the same Lord. In evangelical reading, there is also a typological resonance with the suffering Messiah, without the psalm losing his own voice as David's prayer.

scholarViews.insight: The psalmist appeals to God to remain faithful to his own character; therefore, the basis of hope is divine mercy and forgiveness, not the deserved human dignity.
The psalm can be read as a prayer of David and, in a typological sense, as an expression of the "forts supplications" of Christ in his days of flesh, uniting petition and praise.
The request for a sign of goodness is understood as a visible gesture of belonging and favor, so that the enemies may recognize that God is with his servant.

questions: In what situations do I usually ask for God's help without first resting in his character, how does the psalmist do?
What does it mean, in practice, to have the "united" heart to fear the name of the Lord and not to live divided among various allegiances?
How can a sign of God's favor today be recognized more by transformation and perseverance than by immediate relief?
study.practice: Pray this psalm personally and honestly: present your affliction, but also name who God is. Then choose a concrete attitude of trust - for example, persevere in a correct decision, ask someone for forgiveness, or maintain praise even before the answer. Throughout the week, note how God consoles, strengthens and guides you, and record it as a testimony of your goodness.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not safely inform the exact historical context of the psalm, so any connection to a specific episode of David's life remains conjectural. Adam Clarke's reference to the possible composition in the time of exile is only an interpretative hypothesis, not a given established by the biblical text or by the notes as a certain fact. Also the typological reading that associates the psalm with Christ is a devotional interpretation, not an explicit statement of the psalm.
